result.summary: The chapter traces the descendants of Arcas, focusing on Auge and her son Telephus, and then on Atalanta, her exposure, her hunting, her footrace with suitors, and her marriage to Melanion. Variant genealogies are noted.

scenes.title: Descendants of Arcas
scenes.summary: The line of Arcas is listed through Elatus and Aphidas down to Aleus and his children.

scenes.title: Auge and Telephus
scenes.summary: Auge bears Hercules' child in Athena's precinct; the land turns barren, she is condemned, and her son Telephus, raised by a doe and herdsmen, becomes prince of Mysia.
scenes.stakes: Auge risks death for impiety; the exposed baby Telephus risks dying.

scenes.title: Lycurgus's line
scenes.summary: The children of Lycurgus and their descendants, leading to Atalanta, are listed.

scenes.title: Atalanta the huntress
scenes.summary: Exposed as a baby, Atalanta is suckled by a bear and raised by hunters. She stays a virgin, kills two centaurs, joins the Calydonian boar hunt and beats Peleus at wrestling.
scenes.stakes: Atalanta faces death by exposure, then assault by the centaurs.

scenes.title: The footrace and the apples
scenes.summary: Atalanta races her suitors and kills those she catches. Melanion wins with Aphrodite's golden apples and marries her; later they are turned into lions in Zeus's precinct.
scenes.stakes: Suitors risk death; Melanion risks losing the race and his life.

scenes.title: Variant traditions and Parthenopaeus
scenes.summary: Hesiod and Euripides give different parentage and husband for Atalanta. Her son Parthenopaeus goes to war against Thebes.

notable_quotes.reason: The famous golden apples that defeat Atalanta in the race.

analysis.text: Exposure and rescue of children by animals recurs in Telephus and Atalanta, while Atalanta resists conventional marriage until outwitted.
Apollodorus compiles competing genealogies, naming sources such as Hesiod and Euripides, showing how varied the Greek myth traditions were.

legacy.text: The race with golden apples became a classic story, retold by Ovid in the Metamorphoses and often in later art.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus, but the real author is unknown; it was likely written in the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: "Seduced by Hercules" is the translator's mild wording; in other versions Hercules forces himself on Auge while visiting Tegea.
Telephus's name is linked to the Greek word for deer or doe (elaphos) and to suckling (thele), so the name records how he was nursed.
"Neatheards" are cowherds or cattle-keepers; "neat" is an old word for cattle.
The Calydonian boar hunt was a famous heroic expedition against a monstrous boar sent by Artemis to ravage Calydon.
A cubit is an ancient measure, about the length of a forearm (roughly 18 inches), so the stake stood about four and a half feet high.
"If the wooer was caught up" means overtaken by her in the race; "his due" means his fixed penalty or prize.
"Taking their fill of love" means they had sex in the sacred precinct, which profaned it and brought the punishment.

context_notes.text: Athena's priestesses were expected to stay chaste, so Auge's pregnancy was a serious offence against the goddess.
Centaurs were creatures half man and half horse, often shown as lustful and violent.
Hesiod was an early Greek poet; Euripides was an Athenian tragic playwright. Their versions show that Atalanta's myth had several forms.

literary_notes.text: Exposure of a child and nursing by a wild animal recurs in the myths of Telephus and Atalanta, marking heroes set apart from ordinary society.
The fast runner who kills her suitors is beaten by her own desire for the fruit, and a trivial lure undoes her.
Their fulfilled love brings a punishment: the lovers become lions, which in ancient lore were thought unable to mate with each other.
